The opt-in --embed-mode neural loads all-MiniLM-L6-v2 from a local cache and runs on the CPU.

articles.question: Do I even need embeddings for search, or is full-text enough?

articles.answer: Do I even need embeddings for search, or is full-text enough? On XERJ's default lexical embedder, full-text BM25 is close: 0.4167 precision at 3 against BM25's 0.375 on 8 judged queries. Embeddings clearly helped only after opting into --embed-mode neural, which moved precision at 3 to 0.6667 and recall to 1.0.

articles.title: What is Reciprocal Rank Fusion?
articles.question: What is reciprocal rank fusion and when should I use it?
articles.summary: Reciprocal Rank Fusion scores a document by 1 divided by k plus its rank in each list. XERJ uses k 60, and this page checks the arithmetic by hand.
articles.answer: What is reciprocal rank fusion, and when should I use it? RRF scores a document by the sum of weight over k plus its rank in every list that returned it. articles.title: What do the xerj autoindex exit codes mean?
articles.question: What does indexer exit code 3 mean?
articles.summary: xerj autoindex exits 0 complete, 3 completed-with-junk, 4 needs-a-decision, 2 usage and 1 on an endpoint or journal failure. Only 4 is asking you a question.
articles.answer: What does indexer exit code 3 mean for xerj autoindex? It means success: the run completed and recorded some junk files. Exit 0 is a clean completion, 4 means the estimate exceeded --max-minutes and nothing was indexed, 2 is a usage error, and 1 is an endpoint or journal failure. Only exit 4 asks you a question.

articles.title: Why autoindex refuses a .zip and asks you to extract it

articles.summary: autoindex never opens archives. A .zip, .tgz, .7z, .rar or .xz is marked as junk with the exact extraction command; the run continues. Index the extracted folder.
articles.answer: Why does xerj autoindex say to extract a zip first? Because autoindex never opens archives. A .zip, .tgz, .7z, .rar or .xz is marked as junk with a reason that quotes the extraction command, the rest of the folder is indexed, and the run exits 3. Extract the archive and run the same command again.

articles.title: Why did xerj autoindex say a dataset was REFUSED?
articles.question: Why did xerj autoindex say a dataset was refused by the server?
articles.summary: When the server refuses one dataset's mapping, xerj autoindex records that dataset's files as junk, indexes every other dataset, and exits 3 with datasets_refused on the terminal line.
articles.answer: Why did xerj autoindex say a dataset was refused by the server? The server answered HTTP 400 to that dataset's mapping. autoindex records the dataset's files as junk, indexes every other dataset, and exits 3 with datasets_refused on the terminal line. Re-running does not fix it; fix the cause and rebuild under a new prefix.

articles.title: Why does xerj autoindex say the server pushed back (429)?
articles.question: Why did xerj autoindex say the server pushed back with HTTP 429?
articles.summary: When the node answers a bulk, or items inside one, with HTTP 429 (its memory circuit breaker), xerj autoindex re-sends the rejected items, waits out the moment, and reports bulk_retries on the terminal line. Only 600 s of re-sends that never clear is fatal.
articles.answer: Why did xerj autoindex say the server pushed back with HTTP 429? The node shed load for a moment through its memory circuit breaker. autoindex lowers bulk concurrency, re-sends only the rejected items, and reports bulk_retries on the terminal line. It exits 1 only after 600 seconds of re-sends the node never accepts, and the same command resumes.

articles.title: When does XERJ kNN use an exact scan instead of HNSW?
articles.question: Why is filtered kNN slower than unfiltered?
articles.summary: A filter takes kNN off the HNSW graph and onto an exact scan whose cost scales with vectors scanned. This page explains when that happens and publishes no timing.
articles.answer: Why is filtered kNN slower than unfiltered in XERJ? The filter changes the retrieval path. articles.title: What a XERJ share-link guest can and cannot reach
articles.question: If I give someone a read-only share link to one search index, can they see my other indices or anything else on the server?
articles.summary: A share-link guest key reads the shared index and nothing else: no other index, no _cat or _cluster, no writes, no scroll or PIT. Each refusal is a live test.
articles.answer: If I give someone a read-only share link to one search index, can they see my other indices? No. A share-link guest key carries read on the shared index only, and a guest route allow-list closes _cat, _cluster, every other index, all writes, and scroll and point-in-time contexts. A live test checked each refusal.
